content: Linalool is a naturally occurring terpene alcohol that is present in a wide variety of flowers and spice plants. It is widely utilized in commercial applications, primarily due to its pleasant aroma, which is described as floral with a hint of spiciness. This compound is also known by several other names, including β-linalool, linalyl alcohol, linaloyl oxide, p-linalool, allo-ocimenol, and 2,6-dimethyl-2,7-octadien-6-ol. Natural Occurrence Linalool is produced by over 200 plant species, predominantly from the Lamiaceae family (which includes mints and aromatic herbs), the Lauraceae family (such as laurels, cinnamon, and rosewood), and the Rutaceae family (citrus fruits). Additionally, it is found in birch trees and other plants that thrive in climates ranging from tropical to boreal regions. Interestingly, linalool has also been identified in certain fungi. Enantiomers Linalool contains a chiral center at the C3 position, resulting in two stereoisomers: (S)-(+)-linalool, also known as licareol, and (R)-(–)-linalool, referred to as coriandrol. The (S)-(+)-linalool enantiomer has the CAS number 126-90-9 and is cataloged in PubChem as 67179, while the (R)-(–)-linalool enantiomer has the CAS number 126-91-0 and is listed in PubChem as 13562. Both enantiomers occur naturally in various plants. For instance, (S)-(+)-linalool is a major component of the essential oils derived from coriander seeds (Coriandrum sativum, family Apiaceae), palmarosa, and sweet orange flowers (Citrus sinensis, family Rutaceae). Conversely, (R)-(–)-linalool is found in lavender (Lavandula officinalis, family Lamiaceae), laurel (Laurus nobilis, family Lauraceae), and sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum, family Lamiaceae), among others. The two enantiomers elicit distinct neural responses in humans, leading to their classification as having different olfactory characteristics. The (S)-(+)-linalool enantiomer is perceived as sweet, floral, and reminiscent of petitgrain, with an odor detection threshold of 7.4 parts per billion (ppb). In contrast, the (R)-(–)-linalool enantiomer is described as woody and lavender-like, with a significantly lower odor threshold of 0.8 ppb. Biosynthesis In higher plants, linalool, like other monoterpenoids, is synthesized from isopentenyl pyrophosphate via the universal isoprenoid intermediate geranyl pyrophosphate. This process is mediated by a class of membrane-bound enzymes known as monoterpene synthases. Among these enzymes, linalool synthase (LIS) has been specifically identified as responsible for producing (S)-linalool in various floral tissues. Applications Linalool is extensively used as a fragrance component in a wide range of household products, including soaps, detergents, shampoos, and lotions. Beyond its role as a scent, linalool also serves as a chemical intermediate in industrial processes. One notable derivative of linalool is Vitamin E, which is synthesized through downstream chemical reactions involving this compound.
